analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on large inheritances, eases rules for small businesses, and raises the workweek threshold for employer health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee — introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to five committees, it died without a single vote when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This grab-bag bill would repeal the federal estate tax entirely, let employers treat 40 hours — instead of 30 — as full-time under the Affordable Care Act, and hand small businesses a set of breaks: no fines for first-time paperwork violations, tax-deductible start-up savings accounts, and easier recovery of legal fees when they beat the IRS in court. It also makes it easier to sanction people who file lawsuits. The bill never advanced: it was referred to five House committees and died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates gain the most, since the estate tax by design applies only to multi-million-dollar inheritances and the bill would abolish it outright, while locking in a 35% top gift-tax rate with a $5 million lifetime exemption. Employers of hourly workers gain because a 40-hour full-time threshold for the ACA employer mandate means fewer coverage obligations and penalties for workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours. Small businesses gain real but narrower benefits: no civil fines for first-time paperwork violations (unless the violation endangers public health or safety, hides crime, or goes unfixed for six months), new tax-deductible start-up savings accounts of up to $10,000 a year, the right to recover legal costs from the IRS when they prevail regardless of net worth, and tripled damages for reckless or intentional IRS misconduct. Defendants in civil suits also gain from mandatory sanctions on losing filers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy heirs, employers, and small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax outright, so heirs of the largest estates would owe no federal estate tax at all, and locks in a 35% maximum gift-tax rate with a $5 million lifetime exemption, adjusted for inflation.

Bars federal agencies from imposing civil fines on a small business for a first-time paperwork violation unless the violation could seriously harm the public, conceal criminal activity, endanger health or safety without a 24-hour fix, or go uncorrected for six months.

Creates Small Business Start-Up Savings Accounts with tax-deductible contributions of up to $10,000 a year ($150,000 lifetime) and tax-free withdrawals for startup costs like equipment, facilities, marketing, training, incorporation, and accounting fees.

Lets small businesses with average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less recover attorney fees and costs from the IRS whenever they prevail in a tax dispute, without meeting the net-worth limit that individuals face, and triples the civil damages available for reckless or intentional IRS misconduct to $3 million (from $1 million) while extending the deadline to sue from two years to five.

Raises the Affordable Care Act full-time threshold from 30 to 40 hours a week, sparing employers from coverage obligations and penalties tied to workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours, and changes the formula for counting part-timers toward large-employer status.

Directs the Labor Department to study whether occupational licensing rules hurt service quality, raise consumer costs, and block entry into small business, and expresses Congress's support for interstate licensing reciprocity so licensed workers can move across state lines.
Requires courts to sanction attorneys, law firms, or parties who make false representations to the court under Rule 11, with sanctions paid to the injured party to compensate them.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose estate and gift tax revenue — money that must be replaced by other taxes or borrowing — along with the cost of the new start-up account deductions. Workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours a week would bear the risk of losing employer health coverage offers if employers cap their hours below the new 40-hour line, leaving them to buy their own insurance or turn to subsidized marketplace plans. People who file civil lawsuits would face a higher chance of paying the other side's legal fees under mandatory Rule 11 sanctions. Taxpayers generally would also cover the cost of higher damages awards against IRS employees.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury and hourly workers under 40 hours

drawbacks.text: The estate tax applies only to the largest estates, so repealing it would deliver its entire benefit to wealthy heirs while stripping federal revenue that other taxpayers would have to make up through higher taxes or more borrowing.

Moving the full-time line from 30 to 40 hours gives employers a reason to cap workers at 39 hours to avoid the coverage mandate; those workers lose employer coverage and would have to buy their own insurance or rely on subsidized marketplace coverage, shifting costs to them and to the federal budget.

Making Rule 11 sanctions mandatory, including an order to pay the other side's reasonable attorney fees, raises the cost of losing a legal argument and could deter people with fewer resources from bringing legitimate claims; the bill's own text adds a clause insisting nothing in it should impede new claims or civil rights laws, an acknowledgment of that risk.

The start-up savings account deduction is worth the most to people who can already set aside $10,000 a year, and the accounts must be held by a bank or an approved trustee, so the benefit skews toward those with existing savings and banking relationships.

The 24-hour cure window means a business whose paperwork violation presents a danger to public health or safety can escape a fine entirely by fixing it within a day, and the agency head may waive the fine in other health-and-safety cases after weighing the circumstances.
The package bundles together seven unrelated policy areas, which is why it was split among five committees — a structure that made it easy for any one committee to bury the whole bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The small-business and taxpayer-protection pieces are real: shielding firms from first-time paperwork fines, letting them recover fees when they beat the IRS, and strengthening remedies for IRS misconduct would help firms and individuals who fight the agency. But the bill's largest provision by far is a full estate tax repeal that benefits only multimillion-dollar inheritances, and the 40-hour change shifts health coverage costs from employers onto hourly workers and federal subsidies. The tort provisions would make suing more expensive for ordinary plaintiffs. On balance the package is weighted toward the wealthy and employers, and since it never received a vote, none of its effects — good or bad — ever took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — five of them, in fact — and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on April 14, 2016 with no cosponsors — not one other member of either party signed on.

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Small Business, Education and the Workforce, and Judiciary — because its provisions sprawled across tax, health, tort, and regulatory law, giving each committee only partial jurisdiction.
On May 17, 2016 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, and no committee, subcommittee, or floor vote ever followed.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired with it; none of its provisions — the estate tax repeal, the 40-hour threshold, the small-business breaks — ever took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained, because nothing passed: the estate tax continued to apply to large estates, employers still had to count 30 hours as full-time for health coverage, plaintiffs kept the current lawsuit-sanction rules, and small businesses received no new relief. The main beneficiary of the bill's death was the federal Treasury, which kept estate and gift tax revenue the bill would have eliminated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The estate tax and 30-hour rule survived

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there was no record of who supported or opposed it; the only signal is that the sole sponsor was a Republican and no member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.note: Full repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes, plus a permanent 35% gift-tax rate and $5 million lifetime exemption, would be worth the most to families with multimillion-dollar estates — the only ones that pay these taxes. The lost revenue falls on other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Employers of hourly and part-time workers
industries.note: Raising the ACA full-time threshold to 40 hours cuts employers' coverage obligations and penalties for the 30-to-39-hour workforce. The cost shifts to those workers, who may lose employer coverage and fall back on individual insurance or federal subsidies.

First-time paperwork fines are suspended, new tax-deductible start-up savings accounts are created, and firms with up to $50 million in receipts can recover legal fees when they prevail against the IRS, plus tripled damages for IRS misconduct. These provisions are the bill's genuine Main Street core, though the estate tax repeal at the top does not benefit most small firms.

Mandatory Rule 11 sanctions, including paying the winning side's attorney fees, raise the risk and cost of filing suit. Defendants — often insurers and larger companies — benefit from the added deterrence, while legitimate claims by individuals with fewer resources become riskier.
Start-up savings accounts must be held by a bank or an approved trustee, and retirement-plan rules are adjusted, creating a modest new account-administration business for financial institutions.
